extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of legal history, comparative law, and social science
extracted.subtask_description: Methodological guidance for doing comparative jurisprudence: what to study, how to compare legal systems, and which non-legal facts and historical mentalities must be included to explain legal development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative method — study of evolution and comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: "Social phenomena ... can not be explained by merely physical phenomena ... The most distinct characteristics which they possess lie in their capacities for continuous evolution and development; and it is only by the study of their evolution, by the comparison of their consecutive states, and of each state with the coexisting general condition of society, that we can rationally hope to reach an adequate knowledge of their laws." (Flint, quoted)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare consecutive historical states of a social phenomenon and each state against the broader social conditions in which it existed. Emphasize historical development rather than static description; avoid treating laws as isolated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad comparative scope — study many systems and their histories
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires not only the study of English, ancient and modern Roman, Greek, and Hindoo law, but the study of the history of each; and the comparison of each with all of the others in such manner as accurately to learn their relations to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble cross-cultural and cross-temporal material (multiple legal systems and their historical trajectories). Use wide comparative samples to detect relations and common features rather than relying on a single tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study law on both statical and progressive sides
rubrics_metrics.description: "This method implies the study of law upon both its statical and its progressive sides,"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze both the structure of law at particular moments (statical) and the processes and trajectories by which law changes (progressive). Balance synchronic description with diachronic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose motives and processes of legal development
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure of the motives and processes of legal development is regarded as the most valuable fruit of comparative jurisprudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to identify causal forces and social motives (religious, economic, cognitive) that produced legal change, not merely cataloging norms. Prioritize explanatory accounts that reveal why institutions evolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-legal social facts (religion, ceremonials, customs, polities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative jurisprudence deals with religions, ceremonials, customs, and polities because it reaches back to a time when these and law were but slightly differentiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate data on rites, liturgies, prayers, moral ordinances, kinship, and political organization when explaining legal phenomena. Treat law as interpenetrating with other social facts rather than autonomous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruct primitive modes of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: We must make an effort to reconstruct primitive man on his intellectual side ... and then to think as he thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt cognitive and cultural reconstruction of earlier mentalities (beliefs about sleep, dreams, life/death, causation) to understand legal motives such as ancestor-worship. Use anthropological, mythological, and psychological evidence to avoid presentist misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate ultimate social causes in religious principle (ancestor-worship)
rubrics_metrics.description: The constituent bond of the family ... finds its ultimate reason in religious principle and practice; ancestor-worship is the actual governing motive of native Indian jurisprudence ... the deification of the dead is the oldest religion known to men, which religion is the efficient cause of ancient social organization, the essential principle of archaic institutions, archaic morals, and archaic laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tracing origins of archaic institutions (family, property arrangements), prioritize investigation of underlying religious beliefs (e.g., ancestor-worship) rather than assuming purely political or economic explanations like paterfamilias or simple kinship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use philology and mythology as preparatory evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative study of languages and mythology provided necessary preparation — 'language and mythology form the vestibules and outer courts' — before a successful essay could be made in comparative jurisprudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ linguistic and mythological comparison as foundational tools: philological correspondences and mythic parallels can indicate deep historical connections and should inform legal-historical hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject presentist and speculative system-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Much prior speculation was wrong because modern thinkers assumed elements (states, parliaments, positive laws) as prerequisites for society; the comparative method rectifies these century-old misconceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extrapolating modern legal concepts (contract, individual property, centralized state) back onto archaic societies. Critically examine assumptions and be prepared to discard inherited doctrines that impose modern structure on past societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify laws originally common (mark off 'Aryan law')
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare systems to mark off with something of precision those laws and political institutions which originally they all possessed in common, and which might fairly be denominated Aryan law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative cross-system analysis to isolate features that are genuinely ancestral/shared versus those that are later developments. Seek criteria to distinguish inherited commonalities from convergent or later innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to physical and spiritual conditions antecedent to law
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisprudence requires knowledge of 'the group of conditions necessary for the physical and spiritual development of man so far as these conditions are dependent on human will,' and of physical and spiritual conditions which predetermine law, and to which man has been no voluntary party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include environmental, biological, and cultural determinants in causal accounts of legal institutions. Do not ignore non-volitional antecedent conditions (climate, subsistence, demography, cognitive capacities) that shape social forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish comparative jurisprudence from comparative legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawyers and legislators use the term to mean a comparison of the legal systems of distinct and highly developed societies to facilitate legislation (comparative legislation); comparative jurisprudence, as used here, covers a much wider field than the field of positive law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about aims: whether the inquiry is scientific/historical (seeking origins and development across varied societies) or practical (seeking models for legislative borrowing). Do not conflate the two objectives.
